articles.body: Piddington, a central English village of 350 people, held a symbolic "independence referendum" on Tuesday to protest against plans to house more than 1,200 asylum seekers at a nearby disused military site.The Oxfordshire village, 25km from Oxford, asked residents to vote "Yes" or "No" on whether it should seek to secede from the UK and pursue self-determination. The result is due on Wednesday morning.The tongue-in-cheek vote has no legal basis but residents said it was intended to draw attention to their concerns. Villager Ian Darby (63) said Piddington was willing to accept its share of migrants but considered the proposed number excessive.A govt factsheet said the site would house single adult male asylum seekers for at least 10 years, with the safety and security of migrants, staff and the local community of the utmost importance. Villagers, however, said the plan was impractical because Piddington had only a village hall, a 12th-century church and a playing field.McNally said residents were concerned not about most asylum seekers but about an unpredictable "small minority of individuals who will be a nuisance that we cannot predict or control". He said plans were being considered for CCTV and a village security audit.In an open letter to Parliament's 266 women MPs, 133 female residents said they feared for their safety. Student and part-time stablehand Dita Jackson (17) said she was taking self-defence classes, while farmer Jennifer Owen (76) said the plan would completely change the village.Protests against housing asylum seekers in hotels and other facilities have been held across the UK as irregular migration has become a major political issue. articles.title: Did Russia try and take out Zelenskyy? Ukrainian president says Russian drones targeted his jet twice
articles.summary: Europe News: Russian drones had reportedly targeted the plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy twice in recent weeks, with the Ukrainian leader tel.
articles.body: Russian drones had reportedly targeted the plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy twice in recent weeks, with the Ukrainian leader telling CBS News that the incidents were part of Moscow’s efforts to intimidate him and other foreign leaders.In an exclusive interview with CBS News on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said his presidential jet was targeted while he was travelling through Moldova and again when he was returning to Ukraine a few days later.“In Moldova, my presidential jet was there, and that's why they attacked Moldova,” Zelenskyy told CBS News. “When we went back home, again through Chisinau, they did the same.”The second incident had not previously been reported. Zelenskyy said one or two drones entered Moldovan airspace during the return journey. Ukrainian officials had said at the time that members of the presidential delegation were safe, but it was unclear whether the incident was intentional.The first incident had been publicly disclosed earlier by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who said Zelenskyy’s plane was “almost hit” by a drone while flying through Moldovan airspace on September 9, as the Ukrainian president travelled to Oslo. He added that the incident reflected the reality of the threats Zelenskyy faces.Zelenskyy links drone attacks to foreign leadersZelenskyy also told CBS News that Russia was using drone attacks to intimidate foreign officials visiting Ukraine.On Sunday, a Russian drone struck a passenger train carrying foreign dignitaries travelling in Ukraine, forcing passengers to evacuate near the Polish border. The delegation included senior European officials and former CIA Director David Petraeus.Zelenskyy said he believed Russia may have known that Americans and Europeans were aboard the train.“Maybe they didn't know that some Americans had been there or maybe, oppositely, they knew, because I don't trust them,” he told CBS News.The incident came amid a wider increase in drone incursions into European airspace.Unidentified drones, some of which have been traced to Russia, have increasingly entered the airspace of European countries bordering Ukraine and Russia, according to CBS News.Nato fighter jets on Tuesday shot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace for the first time, the Associated Press reported, citing Lithuanian military officials.Romania has also faced repeated drone incursions since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. In May, a Russian drone struck the roof of an apartment building in the Romanian city of Galați after entering the country's airspace during a Russian attack on targets near the Ukrainian border.Two people suffered minor injuries and were treated for abrasions, while two Romanian F-16s were scrambled after the drone was detected, according to Romanian authorities.Nato subsequently accused Russia of reckless behaviour and pledged to defend “every inch of Allied territory”. Romania also said its allies would provide additional equipment to strengthen its air defences.Russia did not immediately comment on the incident. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by state-run TASS as saying Russian President Vladimir Putin had been informed about the drone strike.Poland also reported shooting down Russian drones in its airspace during a Russian attack on Ukraine last September.The threat has not been limited to Russian drones, with Ukraine's drones also having crossed bordersLatvia recently faced a political crisis after stray Ukrainian drones entered its territory. The drones were believed to have been knocked off course by Russian electronic jamming and caused little damage, but the incidents raised concerns over the ability of Nato's eastern members to detect and respond to drones crossing their borders.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 133-year-old tree with historic carvings may be removed from a protected US forest by helicopter for a museum display
articles.summary: US News: A 133-year-old tree in Wyoming’s Washakie Wilderness has sparked a dispute over how historic sites should be preserved in protected wilderness. The tr.
articles.body: A 133-year-old tree in Wyoming’s Washakie Wilderness has sparked a dispute over how historic sites should be preserved in protected wilderness. The tree bears names carved by a survey crew that became stranded in a snowstorm while marking the Yellowstone Forest Reserve 133 years ago. The US Forest Service approved a plan to cut down the tree and remove it by helicopter for museum display. Wilderness Watch opposes the plan, arguing that removing the tree would harm the wilderness it represents. The group says the Forest Service has already cut other trees and cleared a user-created trail to reach the site. It also raised concerns about limited public notice and engagement, and has urged the agency to pause the project and consider alternatives.Historic tree removal plan may require more trees to be cut for helicopter accessThe planned project involves more than simply removing the marked tree. Wilderness Watch said the Forest Service had already cut other trees and cleared a user-created trail leading to the site. Flooding later damaged a nearby trail, which delayed the work. Under the plan, a state-contracted crew would use the cleared route to bring equipment to the tree and create images that could preserve its history. The next step would be to cut down the tree and remove it by helicopter once one became available after the fire season. Wilderness Watch also raised concerns that more trees might have to be cut to create a landing area for the helicopter.What makes the 133-year-old tree historically importantThe survey tree stands more than two dozen miles from the nearest trailhead in Wyoming’s Washakie Wilderness. According to Wilderness Watch, a survey crew became stranded there in a snowstorm 133 years ago and carved their names into the tree. At the time, the crew was marking the boundaries of the Yellowstone Forest Reserve as part of an effort to protect forests from commercial tree cutting. The reserve later became the Shoshone National Forest. The Washakie Wilderness was established under the 1964 Wilderness Act and expanded by Congress in 1972 and 1984. The Forest Service has since approved a plan to cut down the historic tree, remove it by helicopter, and place it on display in a museum.An alternative way to preserve the tree’s historyWilderness Watch argues that the project goes against the purpose of keeping protected wilderness in its natural state. It reminded the Forest Service that its main responsibility in managing Wilderness is to protect its character. The group also said exceptions that allow prohibited tools are intended to support the purpose of the Wilderness Act, rather than projects that do not serve a wilderness need. It believes the tree can remain where it is while the carved names are preserved in another way. As an alternative, the organisation pointed to fossil replicas in Newfoundland, where replicas can preserve a record without removing the original from its natural setting.How did the Forest Service respond to concerns over public involvementThe dispute also involves concerns over how the Forest Service handled public involvement. Wilderness Watch said the project had not been publicly announced and was not listed on the agency’s website when the group searched for it in July. On August 4, the organisation asked the Forest Service to pause the work and give the public a meaningful chance to respond. The request was denied by a Forest Service supervisor on August 13, who said public involvement was not required. He argued that preserving the story of public lands could help people understand why such places should be valued. Wilderness Watch rejected this reasoning and continued to call for the project to be reconsidered.How will a helicopter be used to remove the historic treeSeveral details about the project were still unclear when Wilderness Watch published its account. The organisation did not know when the tree would be cut, how much work had already been carried out on the non-system trail or whether chainsaws would be used. It also questioned whether the helicopter would need to land inside the Wilderness and whether additional trees would have to be removed to make space for it.On July 30, it submitted a Freedom of Information Act request seeking the project’s decision documents. The group said the Forest Service had not provided the requested documents by the time its account was published, which leaves the key details about the planned removal unresolved.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Killer bahu left out of will’: What triggered Kanpur pharma trader’s murder plot
articles.summary: KANPUR: The 2022 will of 63-year-old pharmaceutical trader Vineet Minocha, which made his wife, son and daughter stakeholders in his property but excl.
articles.body: KANPUR: The 2022 will of 63-year-old pharmaceutical trader Vineet Minocha, which made his wife, son and daughter stakeholders in his property but excluded his daughter-in-law Shalu, is among the key aspects being examined by police in his murder case.Investigators are probing whether the distribution of his properties could have any bearing on the murder.Meanwhile, Shalu’s lawyer, Shivakant Dixit, has questioned the handling of her seized phone, claiming that activity was recorded on its Instagram account at 10.03am on September 6.He has also sought an inquiry into Subrat’s reported visit to a bank on the night of the murder.Police commissioner Raghubir Lal said alleged shooter Vishal Gautam bought the SIM on September 3, two days before Manocha was killed. He used the number to speak to Manocha’s daughter-in-law, Shalu."If Shalu planned the murder, hatched the conspiracy and Vishal purchased a new number for the crime, the question is why calls were made from that number to Subrat," Lal told news agency PTI, adding that investigators were examining Subrat's possible involvement.Police on Monday recorded the statements of Shalu (30), who is currently in jail, and former servant Vishal Gautam after obtaining court permission to question them.While Shalu denied involvement and remained silent on several questions, Vishal reiterated that he carried out the killing at her behest, police said.‘Instagram activity after phone was seized’: Shalu’s lawyer seeks inquiryShalu’s lawyer, Shivakant Dixit, has questioned the handling of her seized phone, claiming that activity was recorded on its Instagram account at 10.03am on September 6. He also sought an inquiry into Subrat’s reported visit to a bank on the night of the murder.Police are also scrutinising Manocha’s properties and financial affairs. Lal said a registered will made in 2022 left his properties to his wife Punita, son Subrat and daughter Shubhani."We have so far found properties in Ghaziabad and Kanpur, including flats on Birhana Road and a property on Canal Road, besides other assets," Lal said.Police are examining whether the distribution of properties had any bearing on the murder. They have also found indications that Subrat was in debt, including online credit and other liabilities, Lal told news agency PTI.Over 300 calls between Subrat, Vishal under scannerInvestigators are closely examining the communication between Vineet’s son Subrat and Vishal, after analysing call detail records of seven mobile numbers. More than 300 conversations were recorded between the two, the highest among the numbers examined, increasing police suspicion of Subrat.Police commissioner Raghubir Lal said around 1,000 pages of call detail records had been obtained for two numbers belonging to Vishal, three to Subrat and two to Shalu.The records cover the period from May 1 until the night of the murder.Investigators are now examining the calls made by the suspects before and after the murder, including their duration and the identities and relationships of the people contacted.The police are also looking into Subrat’s links with Vishal as part of the investigation. Investigating officer and Kalyanpur police station in-charge Keshav Tiwari questioned Shalu and Vishal in jail after securing court permission.Police plan to seek custody remand for Shalu and Vishal and question the two face-to-face with Subrat.Vishal got new SIM, stopped using old number same dayAccording to Lal, Vishal obtained a new SIM on September 3, two days before the murder, and stopped using his previous number the same day. He later made calls to both Shalu and Subrat.Vishal had earlier told police that Shalu instructed him to name Subrat if he was caught, police said.After the murder, Vishal and his aide Rajkishore allegedly escaped from Ratan Orbit Apartment in Indira Nagar by scaling a wall and later booked a taxi.The two also called a friend five times. articles.title: Meta’s ‘spy glasses’ may get a camera-free version soon: Report
articles.summary: Tech News News: Meta is reportedly working on a new pair of smart glasses without a camera, a major change from its existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup. The reported move co.
articles.body: Meta is reportedly working on a new pair of smart glasses without a camera, a major change from its existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup. The reported move comes as camera-equipped smart glasses face growing privacy concerns and bans in places such as schools and cinemas. The new glasses, reportedly codenamed “Luna,” are expected to focus on voice-based AI instead of photo and video recording. According to The Information, Meta could unveil the glasses at its developer conference on September 23-24, with shipments expected to begin in October.As per the report, Luna will have six built-in microphones and a side button that can give users quick access to Meta AI. The glasses are also expected to support Meta's new consumer AI agent, Muse. The speakers are reportedly similar to those used in Meta's current smart glasses.Why Meta glasses are facing privacy concernsThe reported camera-free glasses come as Meta smart glasses face growing privacy concerns. A BBC investigation in January this year identified dozens of accounts that had posted videos of women recorded in public without their consent using Meta glasses. One such video showed the face and phone number of a 21-year-old woman and received more than 1.3 million views.The concerns have also spread to public places. Schools, cinemas and other venues have increasingly banned smart glasses because of the possibility of people being recorded without their knowledge.Luna could focus on Meta AI instead of recordingThe reported Luna design suggests Meta may be trying a different approach to AI glasses. The six microphones could make voice interaction the main way users communicate with Meta AI and Muse. The absence of a camera could also make the glasses more acceptable in places where recording devices are not allowed.Meta's existing Ray-Ban Meta glasses have reportedly sold around 7 million units, showing strong interest in AI-powered wearable devices. The challenge for Luna will be whether consumers find voice-based AI useful enough without the camera features that helped make smart glasses attractive.Meta has already tried to stop hidden recordingMeta announced a software update in July 2026 aimed at detecting when the recording LED has been “physically tampered with or destroyed.” The company said it would block camera recording when such tampering is detected.Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth has also said the recording light was designed so that people nearby could notice when the camera is being used. However, the privacy debate has continued as more people use camera-equipped smart glasses.Developers are building tools to detect smart glassesPrivacy concerns have also led to independent tools designed to identify nearby smart glasses. One example is ZuckOff, a free mobile app developed by Polish developer Pawel Szydlowski. The app uses Bluetooth signals to identify smart glasses that may be nearby.The app can recognise signals associated with devices including Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta and Snap Spectacles. It can provide an approximate idea of how close a pair of glasses is, although it cannot tell whether the glasses are actively recording or identify the person wearing them.Meta expands its AI subscription businessThe reported Luna launch comes as Meta expands its paid AI services. On September 15, Meta announced Meta One, a subscription service offering additional AI features across Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. The company said the service has already reached 15 million subscriptions and trials during its phased rollout. Meta plans to expand the service to Edits and AI glasses.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Court orders North Korea to pay Seoul for blowing up office
articles.summary: A South Korean court on Wednesday ruled North Korea must pay about 44. 6 billion won ($32.
articles.body:
A South Korean court has ordered North Korea to pay about $32.5 million in compensation to Seoul for the 2020 demolition of an inter-Korean liaison office building.

This is the first time the South Korean government has taken legal action against North Korea, but they have no means of forcing Pyongyang to make the payment.

The inter-Korean liaison office in Kaesong was opened in 2018 to facilitate exchange and cooperation between the two countries, but was destroyed by North Korea in June 2020.

A South Korean court on Wednesday ruled North Korea must pay about 44.6 billion won ($32.5 million) in compensation to Seoul for the 2020 demolition of an inter-Korean liaison office building.

South Korean news agency Yonhap reported it is the first time the South Korean government has taken legal action against the North. However, South Korea has no means of forcing Pyongyang to make the payment.

North Korea destroyed the liaison office on its territory in June 2020, following a propaganda airdrop campaign against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un carried out by activists in South Korea.

The office was opened in September 2018 to facilitate inter-Korean exchange and cooperation.

Formally, North and South Korea remain in a state of conflict, as the Korean War from 1950 to 1953 ended only with an armistice, without a peace treaty having ever been signed.

The Kaesong site was one of the few tangible steps taken by the two countries to strengthen ties. It was intended as a venue for discussing bilateral relations and - eventually, Seoul hoped - talks about ending Pyongyang's nuclear programme.

articles.title: How FBI busted Russian plot to kill US-based dissident, target Ukraine supporters
articles.summary: US News: The FBI has disrupted an alleged Russian intelligence operation to assassinate a prominent Russian dissident believed to be living in Washington, DC, .
articles.body: The FBI has disrupted an alleged Russian intelligence operation to assassinate a prominent Russian dissident believed to be living in Washington, DC, after operatives recruited a person in the US to conduct surveillance on the target.According to an Associated Press report, five people have been charged after a Manhattan federal court unsealed an indictment alleging that a Russian intelligence network had been recruiting people in the US and elsewhere since at least 2024 to surveil and kill Russian dissidents.The alleged US operation came to light this summer, when members of the network recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in Brooklyn to surveil and murder the dissident, according to the indictment cited by AP. The recruit was allegedly sent to two locations linked to the intended victim and given explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance.The Brooklyn resident was promised $1,000 and $1,500 for carrying out the surveillance assignments. After conducting the surveillance, the person allegedly provided multiple photographs and videos of locations associated with the intended victim to one of the alleged network members.The operation then escalated to an assassination offer. The US resident allegedly turned down $40,000 offered to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target through murder, authorities said. After the offer was rejected, the alleged Russian intelligence operative tried to recruit other people in the US, offering substantial sums to complete the killing, the indictment said.Russian network targeted Ukraine supportersThe alleged network's activities were not limited to the United States. The Justice Department said its members had also commissioned associates to carry out, or attempt to carry out, acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine.According to the FBI and DOJ statements reported by AP, the network had previously focused on Russian dissidents and defectors, but after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, its activities expanded toward countries perceived as allies of Ukraine. US authorities said members had recently tried to recruit multiple people inside the United States.James C Barnacle Jr, head of the FBI's New York office, said the agency disrupted the plans through what he described as “relentless work.” Darren B. Cox, head of the FBI's Washington office, said multiple FBI field offices, components and partner agencies moved quickly after the threat was identified to disrupt the alleged plot.Five people have been charged in the case. They include Yuri Khrameev, described as a former colonel in the Russian intelligence services, his son Kirill Khrameev, identified as an officer with Russia's Federal Security Service, or FSB, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a Cuban national living in Russia, Yaidel Delgado Suarez; and Angel Eduardo Castro. All five remain at large.The DOJ said all five face a conspiracy charge related to financing terrorism, while Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro also face a conspiracy charge related to murder for hire. The FBI's New York Counterintelligence Division led the investigation, with significant assistance from the Washington Field Office and Homeland Security Investigations.The charges are allegations contained in an indictment. The Justice Department said all five defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Will Smith’s iconic ‘Fresh Prince of Bel-Air’ mansion returns to market with a 25% price cut; famous TV home now listed at $22.95 million and could be demolished
articles.summary: US News: While Will Smith may have quickly shifted from Philadelphia to Bel Air, the move is not as easy as it seems for everyone. His opulent home in 'The Fre.
articles.body: While Will Smith may have quickly shifted from Philadelphia to Bel Air, the move is not as easy as it seems for everyone. His opulent home in 'The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air' is back on sale after a king-sized price cut. Earlier this year, a listing priced the mansion at $30 million which attracted a lot of visitors but zero buyers. Now, the abode is back on the market with a 25% price cut, at $22.95 million, according to a report by Realtor.com.However, what makes the listing even more interesting is that the nearly century-old home's heyday has passed and it would likely be torn down by its new purchaser. This is because it would require a massive amount of work and expenditure to revitalise instead of just building anew. If a buyer were inclined to hold onto the home’s history and keep it standing, its entire nearly 6,500 square feet of interior space would have to be gutted and rebuilt. The outside, so frequently seen in the 1990s pop culture landmark show, would need to support that work.While Smith's uncle and aunt owned the home in the popular sitcom, in reality, it has been owned by Farhad Rahban for nearly 50 years as part of his expansive real estate holdings in the Los Angeles area. He and his wife, Parvin Nourafchan Rahban, raised their two sons, Nicholas and Sasha, there. Sasha, in an interview with The California Post in January, said he was able to watch O.J. Simpson, who lived two blocks over, begin his slow Bronco ride down a Los Angeles highway in a still-notorious media spectacle before cops arrested him.Not ready to move in yetThe mansion still carries its Colonial Revival grace, including a two-story columned front portico framed by sprawling lawns and towering trees. It is advertised as having six bedrooms and seven bathrooms. While listing images don't show much of the interior, certain shots reveal beautiful mouldings, beamed ceilings, arched doorways and fireplaces. A curved bridal staircase connects the levels. Massive windows also flood the space with sunlight throughout the day.Upstairs, the primary suite has sitting areas, two bathrooms and a massive closet space. Outside, expansive stone terracing, a garden gazebo, a stone arbor and a pool house pavilion are enclosed by lush hedging. It all dates to the 1930s, and stands behind secure entry gates.“This is not merely a home; it is one of the finest land and lifestyle opportunities available on the Los Angeles market today,” the listing adds.“Capitalise on the expansive, flat corner footprint to build a (larger) world-class, multi-structure private estate compound,” the listing said of the land’s practical use. As it stands now, the home “is not in move-in shape,” said Christophe Choo, who has the listing with Coldwell Banker Realty.The property, though, “Is one of the finest locations in all of Los Angeles,” Choo said. Choo said he is already seeing interest since listing the property late last week, with a Beverly Hills couple “flying home early from their European vacation to see it,” and other viewings planned.A famed historyThe home is extremely familiar to the millions of viewers who watched 'The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air' from 1990 to 1996. The series boasted an impressive 148 episodes and launched Will Smith into international stardom.Moreover, it comes with a slew of princely neighbours that are some of the most prominent names in sports, politics and Hollywood. LeBron James has a $23 million mansion in the neighbourhood, while actor and former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger has lived in a sprawling multi-acre Brentwood compound for decades. “Star Wars” and “Indiana Jones” hero Harrison Ford is the longtime owner of a private $12.6 million estate, and Oscar-winner and Goop founder Gwyneth Paltrow has a compound there.Until any decisions are made about the property, it has found a new cast of characters, but with a much less buoyant storyline. The estate is a prime exterior for the Hulu/FX summer hit, “The Shards,” a dark erotic thriller set in 1981 in which a serial killer is hunting rich prep school kids.The estate’s pool is featured as one of the male leads gets drunk by it, strips while walking over broken vodka bottle shards, plants a kiss on his costar’s lips, and then cannonballs into the water and is pulled out unconscious. The property is also where one of the female leads gets attacked, presumably by the serial killer.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Meet Tanishka Aglave, the 17-year-old Valrico, Florida student who built a curry leaf treatment, steam system and AI tool to fight citrus greening; she won $50,000
articles.summary: US News: For Tanishka Aglave, citrus greening isn’t simply a problem that exists in textbooks or agricultural research papers. She watched it take a toll on Fl.
articles.body: For Tanishka Aglave, citrus greening isn’t simply a problem that exists in textbooks or agricultural research papers. She watched it take a toll on Florida citrus growers, including her own family, growing up. The disease has destroyed groves across the state, making what used to be a hallmark of Florida agriculture a hard fight for farmers. Aglave was 17 when she set out to attack that fight on multiple fronts at once. The IB senior at Strawberry Crest High School has come up with a three-pronged approach, which includes a treatment using curry leaves, a localized system for steam therapy, and an artificial intelligence tool to help growers track the disease, states an online report by the Davidson Institute website. Her work has earned her a $50,000 scholarship as a 2026 Davidson Fellow.A personal problem turns into a research projectCitrus greening, also known as Huanglongbing, is the most devastating disease of citrus worldwide. In Florida, it’s led to a dramatic decline in citrus production, straining the economy for growers and threatening an industry that is a hallmark of the state. Aglave’s research started with an odd observation of curry leaf plants, which can harbor the insect that spreads citrus greening without allowing the insect to effectively spread the disease. That finding led her to see if compounds in curry leaves might have properties useful against the bacteria associated with citrus greening. She developed a bactericide based on extract of curry leaves and tested its use by trunk delivery in infected citrus trees. But treatment was just part of the picture.Adding heat to a treatmentNext, Aglave developed a localized thermal therapy system, which aims to improve the treatment’s ability to move through a tree. Around the base, her system employs phase-changing materials and salt chemistries to generate persistent heat. The idea is that it encourages transpiration and increases sap flow through the plant’s vascular network, perhaps helping to distribute the treatment more efficiently. The idea was a lot of experimentation. The first extractions only yielded about 10%, so Aglave had to repeat the procedure many times to obtain enough material to test. She also had problems with the standard trunk-injection syringes, which could leak and damage young trees. While waiting for greenhouse trials to bear fruit, she designed and tested several 3D-printed prototypes before developing a smaller, nonpressurized infusion system.Bringing AI to the fieldThe third part of the project addresses another issue: how do you know if a treatment is really working. While laboratory methods such as qPCR and ELISA can provide detailed information about plant health, they are not always practical for a farmer managing a large grove. Aglave created a web-based computer vision application that uses YOLOv11 and analyzes photos of citrus leaves to measure the visible symptoms of disease. That might provide farmers with an easier way to track trees in the course of normal photography, bridging laboratory research and everyday agricultural decision making.From a high school lab to the groves of FloridaThe research was started by Aglave as a freshman and took over 300 hours to complete, often working two hours in the laboratory every other day after school. Her course work in biology, chemistry, mathematics, statistics and biotechnology provided the foundation, and much of the specialized laboratory work, coding and computer-aided design required independent learning. Her research has earned top awards at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair and has been published in the American Phytopathological Society’s journal, Plant Disease. Outside the lab, Aglave seeks to raise climate literacy and awareness of research among young people. She hopes to pursue a career in the biological sciences and continue developing solutions that have practical benefits to communities.Future plansHer vision is long term and extends beyond citrus. The combination of biological treatment, thermal therapy and accessible diagnostics could potentially be adapted to other bacterial and fungal diseases and vascular plant diseases. But for Florida’s citrus growers, the immediate goal is easier: healthier trees. Aglave’s research is intended to make disease management less costly and more environmentally friendly and provide growers with better tools to understand what’s happening in their fields. For a farming family, that could mean a lot more than a successful experiment. It could be protecting a way of life and helping to preserve an industry that has shaped Florida for generations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UAE cancels visas of thousands of Bangladeshis amid heightened scrutiny
articles.summary: South Asia News: The UAE has cancelled the visas of thousands of Bangladeshis, leaving many expatriates stranded in Bangladesh and unable to return to their jobs, busi.
articles.body: The UAE has cancelled the visas of thousands of Bangladeshis, leaving many expatriates stranded in Bangladesh and unable to return to their jobs, businesses and families in the Gulf country. Bangladesh has taken up the issue with the UAE through diplomatic channels and sought a review of the cancellations.The Daily Star reported that the number of affected Bangladeshis has risen from around 4,000 to 4,800, citing Bangladeshi ministry sources. However, the UAE has not publicly confirmed the figure. Bangladesh’s foreign ministry had said on July 30 that 626 Bangladeshis had faced automatic visa cancellations, while stressing that the cancellations were not specific to Bangladesh and had also affected nationals of other countries.Many affected Bangladeshis had returned home on leave before receiving cancellation notices by email or mobile message. Abul Kalam Azad, who had lived in the UAE for 27 years, told The Daily Star that he returned to Bangladesh on April 7 and received a visa cancellation email on July 24 without any reason being given.The cancellations have affected both workers and business owners. One Bangladeshi told The Daily Star that he had two businesses in the UAE and a wife living in Dubai, but was now unable to return.The UAE is home to around 1.2 million Bangladeshi expatriates, according to Bangladesh’s foreign ministry. Dhaka has been seeking greater mobility and the reopening of labour visas for Bangladeshi nationals.The reasons behind the latest cancellations remain unclear. MS Shekil Chowdhury, chairman of the Centre for Non-Resident Bangladeshi, said UAE authorities had increased scrutiny amid the wider Middle East conflict, including checks related to visa renewals, documentation and social media activity. He stressed that he was not saying these factors directly caused the cancellations.Bangladesh’s expatriates’ welfare ministry has asked recently affected Bangladeshis to submit their details as the government works to establish the scale of the problem. Affected expatriates have also sought financial assistance, rehabilitation and diplomatic intervention to help them return to their previous workplaces.The Bangladesh government has not announced a final number of affected nationals or a confirmed reason for the visa cancellations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
